background.definition: Muscular dystrophies are a group of genetic disorders resulting in muscle weakness. Genetic mutations causing muscular dystrophy can be familial or sporadic. Major types are Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), Becker MD (BMD), facioscapulohumeral MD (FSHD), myotonic MD, limb-girdle MD (LGMD), distal dystrophy (DD), congenital MD, oculopharyngeal MD, and Emery-Dreifuss MD. DMD, the most common, is an X-linked progressive myopathy characterized by the onset of proximal weakness by 5 years of age that usually progresses to the loss of unassisted walking by the age of 13 years. It is caused by a genetic defect that leads to a total or near total absence of dystrophin, a protein necessary for normal muscle function.

list.listitem: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD): 1:3000 to 1:3500
The incidence of DMD was 1.07 to 2.77/10,000 based on worldwide population-based data.
DMD/Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD): estimated 1/5,000 males ages 5-9 years; prevalence of DMD is three-fold higher than BMD (2021 data from CDC).

Pooled prevalence rates of DMD and BMD worldwide are 4.8 (95% CI 3.6-6.3) and 1.6 (95% CI 1.1-2.4) per 100,000 males, respectively. Prevalence rates were highest in the Americas at 5.1 (95% CI 3.4-7.8) per 100,000.
Facioscapulohumeral MD (FSHD): 1:15,000-20,000
Limb girdle MD (LGMD): 0.07-0.43/100,000
Yearly average cost for medical care for privately-insured individuals with any type of MD in 2004 was $18,930 ($13,464 at 5 through 9 years of age to $32,541 at 15 through 19 years of age).
DMD is the most common muscular dystrophy of childhood.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 23 studies found a prevalence of neuropsychiatric disorders in patients with DMD of 7.0% for autism spectrum disorders (ASDs), 18.0% for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), 11.0% for depression, 24.0% for anxiety disorders, and 12.0% for obsessive-compulsive disorders (OCD). Among those with BMD, prevalence rates were 6.0% for ASDs, 28.0% for ADHD, 7.0% for depression, 25.0% for anxiety disorders, and 7.0% for OCD.
The prevalence of epilepsy, based on a random effects meta-analysis including 8 studies, was 5% (95% CI 2%-8%) in DMD and 7% (95% CI 3%-11%) in BMD.
With a relatively frequent occurrence and increasing life expectancy for those affected, a primary care provider can expect to take care of one to several families affected by DMD.
DMD is an X-linked recessive with frequent sporadic mutations.
BMD is also X-linked while FSMD, LGMD and most forms of DD are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
There are two genetically distinct forms of FSMD, both resulting from a contraction of a DNA repeat sequence, termed D4Z4 repeat.

In a multicenter French study of 314 children with pediatric myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), 55% were congenital, 31% infantile, and 14% had the juvenile form. Paternal transmission was observed in 13% of those with congenital DM1.
DMD is caused by a mutation of the Xp21 gene coding for dystrophin. There is a high rate of sporadic mutation; two thirds of patients do not have a family history of disease.
DMD is an X-linked recessive defect; therefore, boys are mainly affected. Female carriers may show some manifestations of disease, including weakness and cardiomyopathy.

Dystrophin is required to form a glycoprotein complex linking the muscle fiber cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Absence of the protein leads to degradation of the muscle fiber, which may be further aggravated by an induced immune response.

LGMDs are caused by a number of genetic mutations, some with autosomal dominant and some with autosomal recessive heritance; those associated with cardiac features are reviewed in the cited reference.

LMNA gene mutations, encoding the structural proteins lamin A and lamin C, can cause several phenotypes. In one case series of 78 patients, diagnoses included LGMD, congenital MD, Emery-Dreifuss MD, and atypical myopathy; all shared a similar cardiac impairment.

FSHD is an autosomal dominant disorder; up to 30% of cases are sporadic mutations. It is caused by aberrant expression of the DUX4 gene in skeletal muscle. In a laboratory study of human FSHD muscle, dysregulated fibroadipogenic progenitors accumulated in affected muscles which provides a mechanism for the replacement of muscle by fibrosis and fat.
Give the pneumococcal vaccine and annual influenza vaccinations at recommended intervals. C
Monitor patients for signs of cardiomyopathy (weight loss, cough, nausea, orthopnea, increased fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance). C
Routinely monitor for other respiratory disorders, such as sleep apnea, aspiration, reflux, asthma, and infections. C
Routine screening is not recommended.
Mothers of patients with DMD should be offered genetic testing to determine if they are carriers; adult sisters and maternal aunts may also be carriers.
Female carriers should have regular cardiac screening to monitor for the development of dystrophin-linked cardiomyopathy.
Patients with DMD should receive the pneumococcal vaccine and annual influenza vaccinations.
Patients should be routinely screened for signs of cardiomyopathy, including weight loss, cough, nausea, orthopnea, increased fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance.
Patients should be routinely screened and treated for other respiratory disorders, such as sleep apnea, aspiration, reflux, asthma, and infections.

Although mechanical dyssynchrony was demonstrated in 17.1% of patients with DMD and low EF, and 31.2% of patients with DMD and abnormal EF and fibrosis, all but 1 patient had normal QRS (suggesting absence of mechanical dyssynchrony) making them unlikely to benefit from cardiac resynchronization therapy.

Patients receiving glucocorticoids should be given prophylactic doses of calcium and vitamin D to avoid osteoporosis and fractures. Consider use of bisphosphonates for patients on long-term steroids. In an RCT including 62 boys between age 6 and 16 years with glucocorticoid-dependent DMD, those receiving 5 zoledronic acid infusions over 18 months plus calcium and vitamin D had significantly higher BMD at the lumbar spine at 12 and 24 months compared with those taking calcium and vitamin D alone. Although numbers are too small to assess fracture risk, 5 children in the control group developed Genant 3 vertebral fractures vs. 0 in the intervention group. Mobility and pain were similar between groups.
Lung volume recruitment physiotherapy slows the decline in forced vital capacity seen in patients with DMD.
Infants may be mildly hypotonic at birth and may have mildly delayed gross motor milestones during infancy. By 5 years of age, proximal greater than distal weakness becomes clinically evident. C
If the creatine kinase (CK) level is elevated, perform DNA analysis and/or muscle biopsy. C

The diagnostic criteria include the onset of proximal weakness by the age of 5 years, loss of unassisted walking by 13 years, 10-fold or greater elevation of serum CK, completely absent or almost absent dystrophin on muscle biopsy, and the Duchenne-type mutation in the dystrophin gene. C
Patients with suspected FSHD can be diagnosed based on a genetically-confirmed first degree relative or through genetic testing for presence of D4Z4 contraction. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Age of onset, pattern of weakness, normal dystrophin on biopsy
Associated findings (cushingoid features, bronze skin, cretinism, rickets)
History of prescribed corticosteroids, NSAIDs, or chemotherapeutic agents
Exposures to botulinum toxin, organophosphates, or heavy metals
Failure to thrive, weight and height less than 5% for age
History of erythema migrans or tick bite
History of infection in mother, failure to thrive, opportunistic infection

list.listitem: Patients with DMD will have all 5 of the European Neuromuscular Centre criteria: onset of proximal weakness by the age of 5 years, loss of unassisted walking by 13 years, 10-fold or greater elevation of serum CK level, absent or almost no dystrophin on muscle biopsy, and the Duchenne-type mutation in the dystrophin gene.
If the leukocyte DNA analysis is positive for a known mutation in the dystrophin gene, it is not necessary to perform muscle biopsy.
For patients with suspected FSHD, genetic testing is performed for presence of D4Z4 contraction.
DMD should be considered in boys with progressive weakness, proximal greater than distal, prior to the age of 5 years.
Infants may be mildly hypotonic at birth and may have mildly delayed gross motor milestones during infancy.

Children with DMD usually have learning difficulties and cognitive impairment. In a prospective cross-sectional study of 196 steroid-naive boys with some form of dystrophinopathy, speech delay was reported in 39% (mean age of speaking was 28 months), learning difficulties in 28%, inattentive-overactive behavior in 8%, oppositional-defiant behavior in 5%, and psychosocial adjustment challenges in 4%.

By 5 years of age, proximal greater than distal weakness becomes clinically evident. Patients tend to develop a lordotic posture, to waddle while walking, and to have difficulty climbing stairs. In addition, patients exhibit a Gowers sign - rolling over to the prone and progressively walking one's hands back and then up the legs to rise from the floor.
Caretakers note that boys have difficulty keeping up with friends and with running, jumping, and hopping. They may also note calf enlargement/pseudohypertrophy.
Weakness progresses until loss of independent ambulation, usually by the age of 13 years.

Sleep disturbances also appear to be common. One case series of 63 boys with DMD found disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep in 29.7% (associated with need to be moved by a caregiver and steroid use), sleep-related breathing disorders in 15.6%, and sleep hyperhydrosis in 14.3%.

In a cross-sectional study of 80 adults with DMD, common symptoms included pain (73.4%), fatigue (40.5%), anxiety (24%), and depression (19%). Authors of a meta-analysis found rates of chronic pain of 65% (95% CI 51%-77%) in DMD, 62% (95% CI 50%-73%) in BMD/DMD, 68% (95% CI 52%-82%) in FSHD, and 60% (95% CI 48%-73%) in LGMD, high study heterogeneity was observed in some diagnostic groups.

Physical examination can reveal enlarged muscles of the calves, buttocks, and shoulders (occurring around age 4 or 5 years); these muscles are eventually replaced by fat and connective tissue (pseudohypertrophy) and loss of muscle mass is seen elsewhere.
Cardiomyopathy (most often dilated but can be hypertrophic) occurs in the late teen years in most patients and can lead to congestive heart failure, the cause of death in about 20% of patients.

Patients with advanced DMD can develop oropharyngeal dysphagia (problems with chewing, moving food or fluids posteriorly through the oral cavity, and swallowing) in part due to macroglossia. In addition, there are reports of impaired gastric motility.

Patients with FSHD typically develop symptoms in the second decade of life with impairment of facial, periscapular, and humeral muscles early in the disease course, although the deltoids are spared. Earlier onset of disease appears to be associated with increased severity. Other manifestations include respiratory compromise, retinal vascular disease with visual loss, hearing loss, and possibly cardiac arrhythmias.

In the French cohort study of 314 children with DM1, musculoskeletal impairment was mild while neurodevelopmental alterations were more common and included cognitive slowing in 83%, attention deficit disorder in 64%, written language delay in 64%, and spoken language disorders in 63%. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 27% and cataracts were identified in 7%. Similar difficulties were reported in a study of 40 Australian children with DM1. These difficulties were more common in the 30 children with the congenital form vs. the 10 children with childhood/juvenile onset - intellectual impairment: 96.2% vs. 90%, fine motor impairment: 76.6% vs. 60%, gastrointestinal disorders: 70% vs. 30%, and impairment in neuromuscular function: 100%; vs. 83.3%.

CK level is greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal. As time progresses, the CK level may decrease as there is less muscle mass to degenerate. In one study, CK and transaminases were shown to decrease with age and loss of muscle function; these tests, combined with age, explained 42.5% of loss of muscle function. Due to this decline, CK levels would be inappropriate for monitoring response to therapy.
Blood leukocyte DNA mutation analysis may demonstrate an abnormality in the dystrophin gene.

Brain natriuretic peptide, when used in combination with creatine kinase, presence and severity of scoliosis, and body surface area, is helpful in detecting early heart dysfunction in patients with DMD.

Upper and lower extremity muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used as a marker of disease severity. Authors of a systematic review of lower extremity MRI found the strongest correlations between motor function and quantitative MRI measurements of fat fraction or mean T2. Similarly, in a cohort study of 119 males with DMD, deltoid and biceps brachii muscles were different in participants with DMD vs. controls in all age groups using proton MR spectroscopy fat fraction and quantitative T2 MRI.

A software-based tool that quantified fatty replacement was developed using lower limb MRIs from 10 different MDs and was able to distinguish between them based on muscle MRI patterns. In this study, the best model obtained a 95.7% diagnostic accuracy, with 92.1% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity.
Electromyogram demonstrates myopathic changes in the absence of nerve conduction abnormalities.
Muscle biopsy definitively demonstrates absent or abnormal dystrophin on immunohistological staining and protein analysis.
DMD may be detected as early as 12 weeks' gestation by chorionic villus sampling and DNA analysis.
For patients with suspected FSHD, genetic testing is performed for presence of D4Z4 contraction.
For patients with undiagnosed myopathies, next-generation sequencing may assist in providing a molecular diagnosis.

Downstream treatments under investigation are those that act on molecular pathways that attempt to reduce sarcolemmal damage (e.g., increase intracellular calcium, reduce mitochondrial dysfunction, increases reactive oxygen species [antioxidants], and reduce apoptosis, necrosis and loss of muscle fibers), muscle ischemia (e.g., vasodilators), chronic inflammation (e.g., anti-inflammatory agents, granulocyte colony stimulating factor) or reduce muscle fibrosis and fat infiltration (antifibrotic agents [pamrevlumab, tamoxifen]).

Glucocorticoids help increase muscle strength and improve musculoskeletal and respiratory function in patients with DMD. Prednisolone or prednisone should be started at 0.75 mg/kg/day. If side effects require a decrease in dose, gradual tapering to 0.3 mg/kg/day will give less, but still significant, improvement.

Authors of a Cochrane review found moderate quality evidence from RCTs that corticosteroid therapy in patients with DMD improves muscle strength and function in the short term (12 months), and strength for up to 2 years. There are limited data on prolongation of walking.

In a 10-year follow-up study of male patients with DMD ages 2-28 years, one year or more of glucocorticoid treatment, prescribed for 311 patients, resulted in increased median age at loss of mobility (2.1-4.4 years) and upper limb milestones (2.8-8.0 years) compared to the 58 patients receiving less than 1 month of treatment. There was possibly a decrease in DMD-related death (9% vs. 19%, respectively).

A 3-year median benefit on postponing loss of ambulation, from age 10 years in non-steroid users to age 13 years among patients taking glucocorticoids, was also observed in the TREAT-NMD global DMD database of 5345 patients with DMD.
A small RCT found that providing prednisone on weekends was as efficacious as daily predniosone.

In a retrospective British study of 270 children with DMD treated with daily or intermittent (10 days on/10 days off) corticosteroids for >1 month or no corticosteroids who were followed for over 5 years, children taking steroids, regardless of regimen, showed improved respiratory function and later development of cardiomyopathy compared to controls (16.6 years and 13.9 years, respectively).

In a single-center, open-label RCT with 72 ambulatory children DMD, the daily-steroid regime at 0.75 mg/kg/day was superior to the intermittent-steroid regimen (0.75 mg/kg/day for first 10 days of every month) on functional measures of Gowers time, nine-meter walk test and average power but similar to the intermittent regimen in preserving muscle strength on manual muscle testing at baseline and after 6 months of therapy. However, adverse effects including weight gain, Cushingoid appearance, excessive hair growth, GI symptoms and hypertension were fewer with the intermittent regimen (total 27% vs. 52.8% with daily dosing).

In a larger 3-year, 3-arm RCT with 196 steroid-naïve boys with DMD aged 4-7 years, both daily prednisone and daily deflazacort were more effective than intermittent prednisone for the primary outcome of rise from the floor velocity, forced vital capacity, and participant or parent global treatment satisfaction; differences were primarily from changes in rise from floor velocity.

In the 3-arm RCT noted above, there were no significant differences in the most-common adverse events – abnormal behavior (34% in the daily prednisone group, 38% in the daily deflazacort group, and 36% in the intermittent prednisone group), upper respiratory tract infection (37%, 29%, and 36%, respectively), and vomiting (29%, 26%, and 23%).

Investigators found incident fractures occurred in 156 of 564 (27.7%) boys enrolled in the the UK NorthStar database (2006-2015) during a median follow-up of 4 years; this corresponds to an overall fracture incidence rate of 682 per 10 000 person-years (95% CI, 579-798). The highest fracture incidence rate was observed in those treated with daily deflazacort (1367 per 10 000 person-years).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 59 studies found that longer corticosteroid treatment was associated with later loss of ambulation (>1 y compared to <1 y; pooled HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.27-0.90) but early treatment start (aged <5 years) may be associated with early cardiomyopathy and higher fracture risk.
Vamorolone (Agamree)

Vamorolone is a dissociative steroid that retains some steroidal activities associated with efficacy, such as physiochemical membrane effects and synchronization of tissue remodeling, but without some of its detrimental side effects. In a phase II 24-week open-label trial of vamorolone in multiple-ascending-doses conducted in 48 boys with DMD aged 4-6 years who were steroid-naive, the 2.0-mg/kg/day dose group had improved muscle function with what appeared to be less bone loss, based on increases osteocalcin, and less adrenal suppression and insulin resistance compared to published study data on glucocorticoid effects.

In a 6-month 4-arm, multicenter RCT including 133 boys with DMD, comparing 2 or 6 mg/kg/day vamorolone with either prednisone or placebo, the primary motor endpoint, change from baseline in time to stand velocity, was met using the higher dose (0.05 [0.01] m/s vs. placebo -0.01 [0.01] m/s; 95% CI, 0.02-0.10). Most secondary motor endpoints also favored the treatment groups. All 3 treatment groups led to increased adrenal insufficiency. Vamorolone was FDA approved in 2023.
Givinostat (Duvyzat)
Givinostat is a first-in-class histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor whose exact mechanism of action in DMD is unknown.

The EPIDYS trial randomized 179 patients with DMD to either givinostat or placebo at 41 sites in 11 countries. It followed patients for 72 weeks and found that givinostat reduced 4-stair climb worsening by 1.78 seconds (p=0.03) and slowed NSAA decline by 1.25 points (p=0.04) over 18 months. Patients were ambulatory at baseline. Givinostat was FDA approved in 2024.

Use of the ACE inhibitor perindopril (Aceon) started between the ages of 9.5 and 13 years in children with a normal EF led to a 27.4% absolute risk reduction in all-cause mortality at 10 years (NNT = 4). In addition to its cardioprotective effect, perindopril also may exhibit action on the respiratory muscles. Consider the combination of an ACE and beta-blocker in patients with early cardiomyopathy.

The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends use of an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker for all patients with neuromuscular dystrophies who have a reduced ejection fraction (EF) and to be considered for all boys with DMD over age 10 years before onset of reduced EF.
The AHA recommends use of beta blockers for patients with neuromuscular dystrophies who have a reduced ejection fraction.
The AHA recommends use of an aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone) for patients with neuromuscular dystrophies who have left ventricular systolic dysfunction to improve survival.

Treatments under investigation are those that act on molecular pathways that attempt to reduce sarcolemmal damage (e.g., increase intracellular calcium, reduce mitochondrial dysfunction, increases reactive oxygen species [antioxidants, discussed in CAM therapy], and reduce apoptosis, necrosis and loss of muscle fibers), muscle ischemia (e.g., vasodilators), chronic inflammation (e.g., anti-inflammatory agents, granulocyte colony stimulating factor) or reduce muscle fibrosis and fat infiltration (antifibrotic agents [pamrevlumab, tamoxifen]). Most of these agents are in phase 1 or 2 trials and successes are few. A 2022 review of these agents and progress to date can be found in the cited reference.
A systematic review of 5 small, poor quality studies found no evidence of benefit for calcium channel blockers.
Tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor marketed for treating erectile dysfunction, did not slow ambulatory decline in an RCT of 7- to 14-year-old boys with DMD already taking glucocorticoids.
There are no effective pharmacologic treatments for patients with FSHD, but pain, observed in about 79% of patients, should be adequately addressed.

Spinal surgery may be considered for scoliosis, but there have been no controlled trials exploring its use. Observational studies have noted an improvement of the Cobb angle, but with an associated post-operative decrease in forced vital capacity and lack of appreciable slowing in the rate of functional decline.

Spinal stabilization surgery is considered when the Cobb angle () reaches 20° to 40°, although it may still be performed with greater curvatures. The Cobb angle measures the curvature of the spine and is derived by first drawing lines parallel to the cortical end plates of the proximal and distal end vertebras. The angle formed by the intersection of lines drawn perpendicular to these lines is the Cobb angle.
A potential advantage of early surgery is greater cardiopulmonary reserve.
Surgery may also be indicated for contractures that inhibit motor function. A systematic review did not find benefit of surgery for footdrop in children with DMD.
For patients with FSHD, surgical scapular fixation may be of benefit.

Creatine supplementation appears to increase lean body mass and muscle strength. In a Cochrane review, patients with muscular dystrophies had a significant increase in muscle strength with creatine and a higher number of patients felt better during creatine treatment.
Idebenone, a synthetic analog of Coenzyme Q10 in the quinone family, reduced loss of respiratory function over one year in an RCT of 121 patients with DMD not currently taking steroids.

Authors of a meta-analysis of antioxidants for DMD found 9 studies that demonstrated improvement in pulmonary function with idebenone treatment (2 studies), improved muscle strength with flavonoids- and omega 3-based compounds (1 study), and clinical improvement in physical activity with coenzyme Q10 (2 studies). The remaining four studies found no benefit over placebo with pentoxifylline, superoxide dismutase, vitamin E combination with penicillamine, or penicillamine alone. Most reported adverse events were mild.

The aim of physical therapy is to maximize muscle function and to delay the formation of debilitating contractures. Passive range of motion, orthoses, and walking aids may be helpful in preserving mobility.

Lung volume recruitment (LVR) physiotherapy appears to slow the decline in forced vital capacity seen in patients wtih DMD.Unfortunately, in a recent RCT of 66 boys with DMD, aged 6-16 years with mild lung dysfunction with an FVC >30% predicted, there were no differences in FVC % predicted at 2 years comparing conventional treatment or conventional treatment plus manual LVR twice daily for 2 years.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend strength training to patients with DMD, but it does not appear to hasten damage. Strength training for foot drop did not benefit patients with DMD, based on one study with 65 participants.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies of exercise including 282 patients with DMD found a significant difference in muscular strength and endurance with exercise training compared with no training and placebo, based on very-low certainty evidence.

In an RCT including 19 ambulatory patients with DMD, an 8-week live, on-line exercise program improved muscle strength more than a home-based video program, but neither improved any functional measures.

Aerobic exercise in patients with FSHD is safe and potentially beneficial. In a small RCT of patients with FSHD, a combined strength and interval cycling exercise-training home-based program delivered over 24 weeks significantly increased 6-minute walking distance and reduced fatigue compared to the control group.

In an RCT of 30 boys aged 6 to 10 years old with DMD, children who received physical therapy were randomized to aerobic exercise training with either bicycle ergometer or treadmill for 20-minutes, three times weekly, for three successive months. Both groups improved in the 6-minute walk test and balance, but treadmill training improved walking capacity and balance significantly more than bicycle ergometer.
Short-term neuromuscular electrical stimulation training of the tibialis anterior muscles in patients with FSHD type 1 did not improve strength or motor function.

In the original description of the disease in 1868, Duchenne commented on some degree of cognitive impairment. Although highly variable and potentially dependent on the type of mutation, many patients with DMD show some level of cognitive deficit requiring individual educational programs and support.
Long-term glucocorticoid use may lead to behavioral changes requiring appropriate counseling.
Patients may need treatment for anxiety and depression.

Patients should be encouraged to maintain ideal body weight. Obesity may impair normal respiration and malnourishment may worsen coexistent respiratory disease. In a retrospective study of weight in patients with DMD, at the age of 13 years, 73% were obese and 4% were underweight, while at follow-up (15-26 years of age), 47% were overweight and 34% were underweight.

Noninvasive mechanical ventilation and assisted coughing may improve survival. Authors of a meta-analysis of 50 papers including 1,412 children across 36 different neuromuscular disorders found lower mortality for children using long-term NIV compared with supportive care across all neuromuscular disease types.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that night-time mechanical ventilation likely prolongs survival and reduces unplanned hospitalization, mainly in patients with motor neuron diseases, and natural history supports a survival benefit of mechanical ventilation vs. no ventilation for those with DMD.

Dystrophin restoration treatments are under investigation and include gene therapies, stop codon readthrough, exon skipping, stem cell therapy and upregulation of dystrophin surrogate proteins. The aim of these treatments is to treat the root cause of DMD. Most are intravenous therapies. An update of these treatments is available in this cited reference.

Gene therapy introduces functioning genes using mostly adeno-associated viral vectors. Patients remain on glucocorticoids to reduced innate immune response; activation of complement is responsible for several serious complications including acute kidney injury and death. Primary outcomes are dystrophin quantification in muscle biopsies and change in North Star Ambulatory Assessment score.

Delandistrogene moxeparvovec was approved in 2023. It uses an adeno-associated virus to deliver gene therapy and has been shown to improve some outcomes, although the outcome of improved NSAA score at 1 year was not different between intervention and control groups.

Stop codon readthrough: About 10% of patients with DMD have a non-sense mutation that results in a stop codon which causes early termination of dystrophin translation. Ataluren is an orally-administered molecule that promotes readthrough of premature stop codons, enabling translation of full-length dystrophin. In an RCT with 228 boys aged 7-16 years with nonsense mutation DMD and a baseline 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) of 150 m or more, investigators found no differences in 6MWD at 48 weeks between treatment and placebo groups, although one subgroup appeared to benefit. Ataluren was well tolerated and most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Other trials are ongoing.

Exon skipping: About 14% of patients with DMD have mutations amenable to exon skipping. This therapy acts on the pre-mRNA and modulates splicing so that causative mutations are skipped and the reading frame is restored. Eteplirsen is one of these therapies; FDA approved eteplirsen in 2016. In a case series of 12 patients, weekly infusions of eteplirsen were given for 240 weeks during which 10 patients remained ambulatory and 2 identical twin patients with more severe disease experienced rapid ambulatory loss but otherwise remained stable with similar progression in other disease parameters to the ambulatory patients. At 4-follow-up, 10 of 12 eteplirsen-treated children were ambulant compared to 3 of 11 historical controls. At 7-year follow-up of 22 eteplirsen-treated children, median age at LOA was 15.16 years. Eteplirsen-treated patients experienced a statistically significant longer median time to LOA by 2.09 years (5.09 vs. 3.00 years, p < 0.01) and significantly attenuated rates of pulmonary decline vs. historical controls. Another drug, golodirsen was investigated in a phase 1/2, 2-part, multicenter trial for long-term treatment in 23 ambulatory patients with exon 53 skip-amenable DMD. At 3 years, 6MWT change from baseline was significantly better in golodirsen-treated patients versus placebo (-99.0 m vs. -181.4 m) and loss of ambulation occurred in 9% versus 26% of controls. Adverse events were mild, with no safety-related discontinuations or deaths.

Stem cell therapy involves allogeneic (donor-compatible cells) or autologous (patient-derived, edited cells) transplantation of dystrophin-producing cells with myogenic potential. Early trials demonstrated safety and some efficacy in dystrophin expression but limited functional improvement. Laboratory studies of genome editing tools, such as CRISPR-Cas9, show promise in functional dystrophin production in cell lines. In a phase 1/2 RCT of intracoronary infusion of allogeneic cardiosphere-derived stem cells (CDCs) in 25 patients with DMD and substantial myocardial fibrosis, intervention patients showed improvement in inferior wall systolic thickening and upper limb function over control patients at 12 months. There were no differences in the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events between groups. In another RCT of 26 patients with late-stage DMD and at least 12 months of glucocorticoid therapy, infusions of CDCs for 9 months resulted in significantly less deterioration of upper limb function compared to placebo at 1 year. Three patients developed infusion-related hypersensitivity reactions without long-term sequelae and one patient discontinued therapy due to a severe allergic reaction.

Upregulation of dystrophin surrogate proteins: Paralogue refers to a pair of genes that derive from the same ancestral gene but reside at different locations in the same genome. Several dystrophin paralogues such as utrophin, when upregulated, appear to improve the DMD phenotype. Trials are ongoing.

The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) recommends against offering patients with LGMD gene therapy, myoblast transplantation, neutralizing antibody to myostatin, or growth hormone outside of a research study designed to determine treatment safety and efficacy.
Authors of the AAN guideline recommend referral of patients with MD to a clinic that has access to multiple specialties designed specifically to care for patients with neuromuscular disorders.
The AHA guideline recommends referral of children diagnosed with neuromuscular conditions to a pediatric heart failure expert.

The 2022 consensus guideline from the Heart Rhythm Society Scientific and Clinical Documents Committee also recommends cardiac evaluation including physical examination, ECG, ambulatory ECG, and cardiac imaging (echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging [CMR]) at diagnosis in patients with DMD, BMD, or LGMD2, with periodic retesting even in the absence of cardiac symptoms. In female carriers of DMD or BMD, they recommend screening cardiac imaging (echocardiography or CMR) in adulthood even in the absence of cardiac symptoms. A permanent pacemaker implantation is recommended, if concordant with the patient’s goals of care and clinical status, in patients with these disorders and any degree of sinus node dysfunction or AV block. Additional recommendations can be found in the cited reference.

Upon diagnosis, children should be referred for a cardiac evaluation, to include ECG and echocardiogram at a minimum. Cardiovascular MRI with late gadolinium enhancement can be considered for the detection of early cardiac involvement in patients with DMD but has not yet replaced echocardiography.

In a study of 40 patients with BMD (age 39.0 ± 13.2 years) and 21 matched controls, echocardiographic measurement of left ventricular (LV) global longitudinal strain, defined as greater than -18%, was present in 31 patients (77.5%) and appeared to be a more sensitive measure of LV dysfunction than LV election fraction (LVEF), which was identified in 24 patients (60%). Both parameters showed moderate correlation with troponin I (ρ = -0.523 and 0.553, respectively) and N-terminal pro-b-type natriuretic peptide (ρ = -0.585 and 0.506), but not with skeletal muscle or pulmonary function. At 2-year follow-up, LV global longitudinal strain significantly worsened while LVEF remained stable.
Authors of the AAN guideline suggest referral of newly diagnosed patients with an LGMD subtype and high risk of cardiac complications for cardiology evaluation, even if asymptomatic.
Children with nighttime or continuous hypoventilation should be referred for noninvasive or invasive ventilation modalities.
In one study, respiratory rate/vital capacity appeared to be the most appropriate predictor for determining extent of need for ventilator support.
Respiratory infections should be treated aggressively to preserve an already diminished lung function.

There is insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of a particular oral-motor therapy for children with DMD and dysphagia. Likewise, there are insufficient data to determine the effect of interventions for dysphagia in adults.
Weakness progresses until loss of independent ambulation in patients with DMD, usually by the age of 13 years.
Prior to current assistive ventilation technologies, death routinely occurred in the second or third decade because of respiratory or cardiac failure.

Survival: Based on 2007 data from four states on males with DMD or BMD, 100% survival from ages 5 through 9 years, 99% from 10 through 14 years, 85% from 15 through 19 years, and 58% from 20 through 24 years.

The most recent data (2022) from 526 individuals identified by the Muscular Dystrophy Surveillance, Tracking, and Research Network, found an estimated median survival time from birth of 23.7 years (95% CI 22.3-24.2). Current use of glucocorticoids, scoliosis surgery, and cough assist was associated with a lower hazard of mortality than non-users. Non-Hispanic Black individuals had a higher hazard of mortality than non-Hispanic White individuals (adjusted hazard ratio 2.09 [1.11–3.92]), although there were only 39 individuals in this race/ethnicity category. Interestingly, no differences in hazards of mortality were observed between ever versus never use of cardiac medication and ever versus never use of bilevel positive airway pressure. Other studies show reduced risk of heart failure and mortality benefit with use of ACE inhibitors.
Patients may have mild hypotonia at birth and may have a mild delay in attaining gross motor milestones during infancy.

By the age of 5 years, proximal weakness greater than distal weakness becomes clinically evident. Patients tend to develop a lordotic posture, to waddle while walking, to have difficulty climbing stairs, and to exhibit a Gowers sign on rising from the floor.
Weakness progresses until loss of independent ambulation, usually by the age of 13 years.
Prior to current assistive ventilation technologies, death routinely occurred in the second or third decade due to respiratory or cardiac failure.
With respect to heart failure, mortality is higher for DMD-associated cardiomyopathy than for other dilated cardiomyopathies.

Based on data obtained from the national health registers of Sweden and Denmark, individuals with myotonic muscular dystrophy are at a 2-fold increased risk of cancer; specifically endometrial, brain, ovarian and colon cancer.

Osteopontin genotype appears to be a modifier of disease severity; those with the G allele (dominant model; 35% of subjects) had more rapid progression. In addition, patients with a single deletion of exon 45 showed an increased survival and increased age (mean 15 years of age) until ambulation was lost in contrast to other single exon deletions. In another study of adults with DM1, disease severity was associated in part with progenitor allele length and variant repeats.

Similarly, among 578 patients with FSHD type 1 enrolled in the United States National Registry, smaller allele sizes were predictive of earlier age at onset, diagnosis and likelihood of wheelchair use; individuals with 1–3 repeats were diagnosed at a markedly younger age compared to those with higher numbers of repeats. Average follow-up was 9 years with a range of 0 to 18 years. Females were more likely to progress to wheelchair use and at a faster rate compared to males, independent of genetics. Median age of wheelchair use for females was 59 years (95% CI 56-62) vs. age 64 years (95% CI 62-68) for males. Over half of participants had achieved a college degree or higher (63.9%), and most were employed at enrollment (52.6%).

The orofacial muscle weakness in patients with FSHD can cause difficulty in swallowing. In one study of 43 patients with FSHD, dysphagia and difficulty with verbal communication were reported by 25% and 35% of patients, respectively. These difficulties were correlated with cheek compression strength and endurance and to anterior tongue elevation endurance.

In a 4-year study of children with COL6-related dystrophies and LAMA2-related dystrophies, Motor Function Measure 32 scores decreased at a rate of 4.01 and 2.60 points, respectively, annually and there was a 3% yearly decline in pulmonary function in those with COL6-related dystrophies.

The use of glucocorticoids and perindopril appears to enhance survival in patients with DMD. In a cohort study of children with DMD on ACE inhibitors with or without use of corticosteroids, prophylactic steroid therapy was associated with a substantial reduction in all-cause mortality and new-onset and progressive cardiomyopathy. Survival rates at 5, 10, and 15 years of follow-up were 100%, 98.0%, and 78.6%, respectively for patients on steroids compared to versus 100%, 72.1%, and 27.9%, respectively, for patients not receiving steroid therapy. There is a case report of a 53-year-old with DMD.

The use of assistive mechanical ventilation may prolong survival to the third or fourth decade. In a Japanese study of treatment evolution and survival over time, the 56 patients untreated (prior to 1984) died at age 18.6 ± 2.9, the 21 patients managed with tracheotomy (1984-1991) died at 28.1 ± 8.3 years of age with 3 still alive, and the 88 patients (1991 plus) managed with noninvasive ventilation had 50% survival to the age of 39.6 years.

The AHA recommends follow-up cardiac evaluation with clinical exam, ECG and echocardiography every 2 years for patients with DMD/BMD who are <10 years of age and annual thereafter. Evaluation every 2 years is recommended for most patients with asymptomatic LGMDs. For additional recommendations, see the cited reference.

At 4 years to 6 years of age, children with DMD should have baseline pulmonary function tests. By the age of 12 years, or when confined to a wheelchair or when forced vital capacity is less than or equal to 80%, they should see a pulmonologist twice yearly. Patients with severe FSHD should have routine pulmonary function testing.

Observations of natural maneuvers such as a sniff or a cough, and measurement of esophageal and gastric pressures during spontaneous breathing can be used to assess respiratory muscle strength and endurance in young children.
Obtain periodic pulmonary function testing for patients with LGMD with a known high risk of respiratory failure.
On loss of walking, children should be evaluated for scoliosis and corrective surgery. Costs and benefits should be weighed in deciding for or against the procedure.

feature.caption: General, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, and Musculoskeletal Care of the Patient With Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

tr.td: Ensure pneumococcal and yearly influenza vaccinations.
Aggressively treat respiratory infections.
Offer dietary counseling to encourage ideal body weight.
Screen for learning disabilities and offer appropriate interventions.
Refer children and parents to one or more of the many muscular dystrophy care groups (see "Suggested Web Sites").
Discuss end of life care with both patient and family.
Obtain baseline pulmonary function tests at 4 to 6 years of age.
Ensure that children are taught and encouraged to use airway clearance strategies early.
Routinely screen for and treat other respiratory disorders, such as sleep apnea, aspiration, reflux, asthma, and infection.

Refer children for twice yearly pulmonology check-ups at age 12 years, or when confined to wheelchair or FVC = 80%. If a child requires mechanically assisted ventilation, ensure that they see a pulmonologist every 3 to 6 months.

Prescribe assisted cough technology for those with difficulty clearing the airway, with peak cough flow <270 L/min, or max expiratory pressures <60 cm H2O. Consider lung volume recruitment physiotherapy to slow declines in forced vital capacity.
Consider noninvasive nocturnal ventilation for patients with sleep-disordered breathing or nighttime hypoventilation.
Consider continuous noninvasive or continuous invasive ventilation when constant hypoventilation develops.
Refer children for a cardiac evaluation upon diagnosis, including ECG, echocardiogram, and other modalities as indicated.
Routinely screen for signs of cardiomyopathy, including weight loss, cough, nausea, orthopnea, increased fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance.
Ensure that children are seen by a cardiac specialist at least biannually until the age of 10 or until overt cardiac symptoms develop. Thereafter, they should be seen yearly.

Consider the early use of perindopril prior to the development of cardiomyopathy symptoms. Once symptoms start, additional medications such as beta-blockers, diuretics, and digoxin should be considered.
Ensure that patients have complete cardiopulmonary assessments prior to surgery. Anesthetic agents that trigger hyperkalemia or hypermetabolic states should be avoided.
Consider anticoagulation therapy for patients with severe cardiac dysfunction.
Refer children to physical therapy to preserve muscle function and to prevent the development of contractures.
Start glucocorticoids to improve muscle strength and function. Prednisolone 0.75 mg/kg/day is the recommended dosage.
Make orthoses and ambulatory aids available to prolong ambulation and to ensure maximum mobility.
Consider surgery for contractures that inhibit optimum muscle function.
Consider creatine supplementation to enhance muscle function.
Consider scoliosis surgery to help improve functional status and quality of life.
